title: Leveraging the Customer Base: Creating Competitive Advantage Through Knowledge Management
abstract: Professional services firms (e.g., consultants, accounting firms, or advertising agencies) generate and sell business solutions to their customers. In doing so, they can leverage the cumulative experience gained from serving their customer base to either reduce their variable costs or increase the quality of their products/services. In other words, their “production technology” exhibits some form of increasing returns to scale. Growth and globalization, coupled with recent advances in information technology, have led many of these firms to introduce sophisticated knowledge management (KM) systems in order to create sustainable competitive advantage. In this paper, the authors analyze how KM is likely to affect competition among such professional services firms. The results shed light on the current literature exploring the deployment of KM systems by suggesting that in a competitive setting, when firms' ability to leverage their customer base is high, KM should lead to quality improvement rather than cost reductions. In a dynamic setting, it is also shown that when firms use their KM system to improve product quality, higher ability to leverage the customer base may actually hurt profits and lead to industry shakeout.
summary_en: Professional-services firms (consultants, accountants, advertising agencies) increasingly invest in knowledge-management systems, and the question is whether these systems are best deployed for cost reduction or for quality improvement. Ofek and Sárváry develop a competitive model showing that when a firm's ability to leverage its customer base is high, equilibrium dictates investing in quality rather than cost. In dynamic settings, very high leverage ability can actually reduce profits and trigger industry shakeout — fitting observed mergers and the rise of 'retail consulting' in the 2000s.
data_used: Theoretical model with empirical anchoring to descriptive industry trends in the consulting and advertising sectors during the 1990s.
policy_relevance: Hungarian innovation-policy programmes that subsidise knowledge-management or digital-transformation investment in the professional-services sector (Digitális Jólét Program, IFKA support schemes) typically assume KM lowers costs. The paper shows that in competitive markets the equilibrium use of KM is quality enhancement, not cost cutting — relevant when calibrating productivity-uplift assumptions in business-case templates for such programmes.
